revisions.text:
The radiator wears its several ribs
inside a coat of old paint.
Heat is the small argument passing
from metal to air, never quite settled.
Under the chair, two slippers point
at a place the wall keeps warm.
Their felt has taken the feet's shape
and rests in it, loosely faithful.
A small coin lies beside one heel,
bright along its least handled edge.
The coin keeps the room's other temperature.
You could close a hand around it
and wait for that to change.
Above the chairs, the clock's second hand
scrapes no paint from its circle.
The radiator ticks behind the slippers;
something expands without finding more room.
There are chairs enough for everyone
who is here, and one more.
Light rests on that empty cushion
as lightly as on a shoulder.
Still the narrow rim receives heat,
still the felt holds a little air,
still the pipes return through the wall.

We move the travel shelf first,
which has never been anywhere
except beside the leaking pipe.
You take the atlas end;
I take the paperback republics.
Behind them, the wall keeps
its narrow receipt of dust,
a rectangle with four pale screw holes.
I write DO NOT PAINT YET
on the back of an order form.
You ask what we're saving.
Nothing, I say, then leave the form there.
From under the bottom board
comes a scrap with an address:
number, street, a town I know
only from the returns label.
Someone has pressed the last digit
twice, correcting it without crossing out.
I flatten the paper on the counter
with the brass bell, which rings
once under the weight of my hand.
We still have poetry to move,
and three boxes marked MISC.
I turn the scrap over. Blank.
There is room for our new address,
but the shop has not moved;
only the books have changed their neighbors.

The platform keeps one shoeprint
where rain has thinned the dust.
A woman at the far shelter
folds a receipt into smaller weather.

Along the blue gutter, water carries
one yellow thread from a broom.
The tram has taken its windows,
its seated faces, its warm rectangle
past the closed bakery and away.

Now the rail gives back a sound
so slight I turn toward it:
a spoon laid inside another spoon,
then nothing I can name.

The woman checks the empty track.
Her sleeve catches on the bench.
She frees it without looking down.

Under the timetable, a moth
holds to the printed Sunday.

The gutter darkens where a leaf
has covered the blue enamel.
Water goes beneath that leaf.

I move my foot out of the rain.
The shoeprint fills, loses its heel.
At the far shelter the receipt
opens once between her fingers.

Beyond the bakery, a window shines,
its edges blurred by rain.
The platform keeps the sound.

At first the ceiling lies together
in the water, beam beside beam.
The drain is somewhere underneath
that room turned gently upside down.

A ladder enters its own ladder.
Each rung waits for the other rung.
Nothing seems to leave until
a tile appears along the wall.

Then another tile. Then the light
separates from its long companion.
A small wave takes the window apart
and lays it down in pieces.

I stand where the shallow end begins.
The painted depth has no reflection.
My hand rests on the metal rail;
I lift it; the rail curves into water.

Water leaving, water staying
in the hollow of a broken tile.
The ceiling gathers at the deep end.
Beside a beam, the clock's two hands move.

No one has moved the chairs.
Their white legs wait above the rim.
A red towel hangs from one of them,
dry almost to its lowest corner.

The last wide sheet divides around
a leaf I had not seen arrive.
Two windows tremble on either side.
Between them, the bottom of the pool.

The instruction was written across the bottom of an invoice for six iron stoves. Above it, the clerk had itemised every hinge. Below it, he had apparently considered three words sufficient to move a winter's provisions.

“By Neral,” Sera read. “Before the mouth freezes.”

Iven turned the sheet towards the lamp. “To Neral.”

Outside the archive window, the second barge was lifting against its ropes. They could hear the loading master calling for the stove crates. If those went aboard now, the flour would have to wait for the evening tide.

Sera laid her pencil across the disputed mark. “The same construction as the eastern passages. By the narrows, by the salt road. It's an instruction about passage.”

“Neral signed the receipt in the next account.”

“Neral is also what they called that channel.”

“After him, perhaps.”

She lifted her pencil. The mark beneath it might have been a shortened destination ending. It might have been the beginning of a letter cancelled by the clerk's own thumb. A brown crescent ran from the word into the margin.

Iven fetched the receipt. There was the name, followed by a flourish and a thumbprint. Sera fetched the coast register, where Neral occupied half an inch of water between two islands. Neither document had a date they trusted.

The loading master appeared in the doorway. “Stoves or flour?”

“We need a few minutes,” Iven said.

“You've had them.”

Sera looked at the invoice again. Six stoves, each with a separate charge for packing. Whoever had ordered them had expected to use them somewhere. Their expedition had brought tents, a surgeon and a surveyor who still refused to say where the northern camp would stand.

“Is the man Neral at Bell landing?” she asked.

“He was yesterday.”

“Send somebody to ask whether he's expecting these.”

The loading master held out his hand. “Write it.”

Iven reached for the dispatch pad. Sera kept her palm on the invoice.

“Don't write that they're his.”

“I wasn't going to.”

He struck through the printed heading, Recipient. Sera lifted her palm. He wrote a question and read it aloud: “Are six iron stoves expected at Bell landing? We have no consignee confirmed.”

“Hold the stoves for the reply. Put the flour aboard,” Sera told the loading master.

Iven tore off the sheet. The loading master folded it into his cap and left. Through the window they watched him stop the crane. Its suspended crate turned slowly, showing them first the shipping mark and then a blank side.

“We haven't translated it,” Iven said.

“No.”

She put a slip beneath the doubtful word and copied both readings. Iven moved the receipt beside the register. Beyond the glass, two men began dragging the stove crates back under the awning to make room.
revisions.work_context: In the invented novel, an expedition gathers at a river port after receiving incomplete supply orders from a northern station. Sera translates regional records; Iven works chiefly with merchants' accounts. Their overlapping expertise has become strained as departure approaches. The expedition's destination, the station's condition and the reliability of its intermediaries remain unsettled. This excerpt covers only their reading of one instruction and its immediate effect on loading.

revisions.text:
Mara put the unsigned delivery slip beside the sugar bowl. Everyone had already seen it; positioning it in the middle made it look newly accusatory.

“The school says we promised thirty crates on Thursday.”

“Twenty-four,” said Ivo. “That was the order.”

“Thirty is what they were expecting. I'm not saying it's what we promised.”

Ada turned her notebook around. THURSDAY—SCHOOL, it said. Below that she had written a name and crossed it out so thoroughly that the paper had thinned.

“I took these minutes. I didn't take the call.”

“Then why Thursday?” asked Tomas.

“Because somebody said Thursday.”

Ivo rubbed the groove his wedding ring had left on his finger. He had removed it before the morning's work and forgotten where he'd put it.

“I said the packing could be finished by Thursday. I was standing in the doorway. I never spoke to the school.”

“I spoke to them,” Tomas said. “Tuesday, from the van. The teacher asked if we could bring whatever was ready.”

“Did you say yes?”

“I said I'd ask.”

“That's not how you told me,” said Mara.

Outside, a crate slid across the loading platform. They all stopped talking until the scraping ended.

Mara had been upstairs on Tuesday, replacing the office printer's feed roller. Tomas had come in while she had the machine open. She remembered his boots on the clean paper she had spread under it.

“You said, ‘They'll take whatever's ready Thursday.’ I put the route on the board.”

“That was why I said Thursday,” Ivo said. “For packing. I don't know what Tomas said upstairs.”

Ada shut her notebook halfway. “I heard ‘school Thursday’ at the meeting. I thought the amount was settled elsewhere. That's why there's no number.”

Tomas reached for the slip, then left it where it was.

“I drove there Thursday with twelve. The teacher said the children had already counted out thirty planting beds.”

“Did she say who gave her that number?”

“No. I was trying to get the crates unloaded before the rain.”

Mara drew three columns on a fresh sheet: heard directly, passed on, assumed. Ada objected to the last heading until Mara changed it to filled in.

They entered twelve under delivered. No one disputed that. Beside promised, Ada wrote a question mark large enough to resemble a hook.

“I'll call the teacher with you,” Tomas told Mara. “I want to hear what she remembers.”

Mara nodded and slid the sheet toward him. Ivo pointed to heard directly. “Packing by Thursday,” he said. Ada entered it.

Under the table, Ivo found his ring caught in the cuff of his trousers. He put it back on without announcing the discovery.
revisions.work_context: The novel follows a nursery cooperative during its first season supplying municipal gardens. Mara coordinates orders, Ivo supervises packing, Tomas drives deliveries, and Ada records meetings while also working on the growing benches. Members are disputing whether informal promises have exposed the cooperative to debts it cannot meet. This scene concerns one school delivery; the school staff have not yet given their account, and the cooperative's wider financial dispute remains open.

revisions.text:
By the time Sela brought the thermometer into the council room, the reservoir had begun its evening change. Its water was seven degrees warmer than it had been at sunset. Outside the windows, frost was whitening the handrail.

“The same rise as yesterday,” she said. “It will hold until dawn. Then it's ordinary water again.”

Councillor Pell pushed the thermometer toward the lamp as though brighter light might improve the number.

“One outlet,” Sela continued. “We can move the hose between buildings. We cannot run two lengths at once. We tried yesterday; neither room warmed.”

“How long to move it?” asked Enid.

“Forty minutes. More if the couplings freeze.”

Enid had brought a tray of cabbage seedlings from the communal greenhouse. Their pale stems leaned over the edges of their cells. She set them beside Pell's papers.

“They don't need to be comfortable. They need not to freeze.”

Joren, who managed the old school shelter, did not put anything on the table. “Neither do the people in the west classroom.”

“The shelter has a stove,” Enid said.

“With a cracked flue. We stopped using it this morning.”

That was new to Sela. She looked at Pell, who looked down at a letter beneath the seedlings.

“The repair request came at four,” he said.

“Then say that at four,” Enid said, but she moved the tray off his papers.

Sela unrolled the hose plan. The school and greenhouse were nearly equal distances from the reservoir. The shelter's radiator held more water and took longer to heat. Once disconnected, it would retain some warmth; she had no measurement for how much.

“Don't put a number in my mouth,” she told Pell when he suggested two hours.

A bell sounded from the street. The shopkeepers were closing early, pulling their shutters against the cold.

Joren asked for the whole night. Enid asked for the four hours before dawn. Pell proposed alternating nights, then fell silent when Enid touched one of the bent stems.

“Tonight first,” Sela said. “We can argue about a week when we have another reading.”

They voted to connect the shelter until midnight, then attempt the transfer. Joren voted against it.

“Twelve-forty at the earliest,” Sela told Enid. “Later if the couplings freeze.”

“So I may not get my four hours.” Enid voted for it and asked what would happen if a coupling jammed.

Sela wrote the question in the minutes, with her name beside it: inspect before disconnecting; if jammed, call Pell before proceeding. Pell folded the sheet into his pocket. She took the thermometer and the hose keys.

At the door, Joren caught up with her. “I'll help move it,” he said. “I'm still against it.”
revisions.work_context: An unexplained nightly warming has begun in the reservoir above a mountain town already short of fuel. The novel follows residents learning its limits while arguing over access to shared infrastructure. Sela maintains the water system, Pell chairs the council, Enid grows communal food, and Joren runs temporary accommodation in the old school. This meeting sets an arrangement for one cold night; the phenomenon's cause and a durable allocation policy remain unresolved.

revisions.text:
Vey laid the old drawing on the keeper's table and weighted its corners with four buttons from her coat. Outside, the bell rope tapped the wall. There was no wind in the kitchen, but the sound made the paper seem liable to escape.

"This neck of land," she said. "I cannot find it."

Keeper Arven leaned over the drawing without touching it. The ink showed a smooth headland joined to the mainland by a strip scarcely wider than the road drawn upon it. Through the kitchen window, water lay between the headland and the shore.

"You came at high tide."

"I came yesterday at low tide. I walked to the end of the road."

He picked up one of the buttons and turned it over. Vey put her finger on the lifted corner.

"The road ends in steps," she said. "The drawing carries it straight across."

"They used a boat for the last bit."

"Then it should show water."

Arven replaced the button. He had polished the stove that morning; its round lid reflected a pale patch of window. Vey could smell polish beneath the fish he had fried for breakfast.

"Where was this made?" she asked.

"Here."

"At this table?"

"There was another table then."

She looked up. He was watching the paper, and she could not tell whether he had misunderstood her or was asking her to abandon the question.

"Where did the draughtsman stand?"

After a moment Arven fetched a key from above the stove.

On the eastern gallery, the iron railing was cold enough to hurt her bare fingers. From there the headland overlapped the mainland exactly. The water vanished behind a shoulder of rock. A path on either shore appeared to meet.

Vey held the drawing against the rail.

"He drew what he saw."

"He was my father," Arven said.

She lowered the paper. Below them a skiff entered the channel she had been unable to see. Its sail disappeared first, then returned beyond the rock.

"Was he making a chart?"

"A prospect for the harbor office. They asked for a view from the light."

Vey examined the margin. Beneath the later survey stamp she could just distinguish the tail of another word, too little to read. She rubbed neither stamp nor paper.

"The stamp makes it look surveyed," she said. "I can't tell what was here before."

Arven fitted the key into the lock of the open gallery door. His hand began to turn it, then stopped. "What will you put on yours?"

She set the drawing on the stair and opened her field book. Between the two shorelines she left a space wide enough to write a sounding.

Vey is a visiting chart maker whose contract requires direct observation of approaches used by small vessels. Arven maintains the isolated light and holds several drawings made by his father. This excerpt covers their examination of one drawing and their visit to the lighthouse gallery.

revisions.text:
The last connection left at eleven forty, while the incoming bus was still showing three minutes away. Ruth watched its number advance along the map. At this hour the little green vehicle seemed to travel through houses.

The passenger came to the dispatch window carrying a folded pushchair. No child, just a carrier bag wedged between the wheels. She needed the estate beyond the hospital. Ruth checked the timetable although she knew it. The passenger waited without putting down the chair, and that made the checking feel worse.

Behind Ruth, Cal took out his phone. He spoke to a taxi firm he knew, then went outside with the passenger. Through the glass Ruth saw him give the driver notes. When he returned, his reflective jacket was open and rain had darkened his shirt.

“Twenty-six,” he said, putting the change in his pocket. “She’s gone.”

Ruth brought up the incident form. She could enter the incoming bus’s delay and leave the connection field blank. The daily total would still be right: seven minutes late. But a missed connection generated a separate line, and somebody on the morning shift had to explain that line to the service manager.

“You got a receipt?” she asked.

“Wasn’t thinking about expenses.”

Cal had held the outgoing bus for four minutes. At eleven forty its driver had called again, asking to leave; Cal had looked at Ruth, and she had nodded. Four minutes was what the standing instruction allowed. Yesterday the manager had asked why the last service was regularly reaching its terminus late.

She selected MISSED CONNECTION. The next box was called passenger disposition. She typed Taxi arranged, fare paid privately, then stopped. That would make somebody ask who. Cal was already stacking the radio batteries for charging, his back to her.

“If I put this through, he’ll want the radio times.”

“They’re recorded.”

“I know.”

She left the words in the box and entered the departure time and her own initials in the authorising field. In the notes she wrote that the passenger had reached the window after the outgoing service departed. She read it twice, checking that she had not made the passenger sound late.

Cal came over when the printer started. He read the report while Ruth fetched an envelope from the drawer.

“Give me what you’ve got,” she said.

He put two coins on the desk, misunderstanding, then laughed once and took them back. From his jacket he produced the taxi firm’s card. Ruth wrote twenty-six pounds and Cal’s name on the envelope, with a note asking the morning dispatcher to get a receipt from the firm and check whether Cal could claim it back. She clipped it to the morning copy.

At midnight the relief dispatcher arrived. Ruth showed him the extra line before showing him the faulty radio charger. Both would need dealing with in the morning.

By the time we reached the lockers, Mara had begun putting everything I said into the category of things that delayed going home. I understood this because she announced the category whenever I spoke.

We had drained the outdoor pool, rolled the covers and carried the lane ropes into the shed. My hands smelt of the ropes even through my gloves. Mara was checking the lockers for towels. I followed with the rubbish sack and the winter checklist.

Inside forty-eight, someone had pencilled I can do it without you on the back panel. The letters leaned uphill. Below them was a pale oval where a sticker had been peeled away.

“Bit grim,” Mara said.

I thought it was encouraging. I told her about a boy I had watched all summer, swimming one length while his mother walked beside him on the tiles. Eventually she stayed at the shallow end.

“Was this his locker?”

“I don't know.”

“Then it could just as well be somebody telling somebody to get lost.”

She found a hair band in the corner and dropped it into my sack. I wanted to retrieve it, though I couldn't have said for whom.

Mara took a damp cloth from her bucket. I said we should leave the writing. She looked at me with the expression she used when I proposed saving cracked kickboards.

“Pencil comes off now. Next year it might not.”

It was her third winter closing and my first. She had shown me how to leave the shower valves, which hinges seized, which cover straps would look sound until you pulled. I had been grateful until about four o'clock, when gratitude began to feel like another thing I ought to be doing properly.

“It's inside,” I said. “Nobody sees it unless they open the door.”

“That's generally how lockers work.”

I laughed, unwillingly. She rubbed a little patch beside the sentence. Grey came onto the cloth.

There were thirty lockers still to check. Rain was coming sideways through the open entrance, and we had left our coats in the office. I held the sack open. Mara moved on to forty-nine without wiping the words.

I couldn't tell whether she had agreed with me or simply calculated that arguing took longer. At the last locker she found a dry towel and wrapped it around her shoulders, label out. I let her wear it all the way to the office before mentioning that.

We signed the checklist together. I put the sack down carefully, though I couldn't see the hair band in it. Under graffiti, I began Message, then crossed it out and wrote One pencil inscription inside locker 48. Mara leaned over and added left in place.

“Now you'll remember where your encouraging boy lives,” she said.

“Our boy,” I tried. She flicked the towel at my knees.

At six, the chess club discovered that its room had become a Pilates studio. Through the glass, Mrs. Bell could see their folding tables supporting a row of lavender cylinders.

“They have put cushions on the rooks,” she said.

“Those are rollers,” said Ahmed, who knew because his wife owned one and occasionally rolled him.

Mr. Vale, the custodian, arrived carrying a bucket. Mrs. Bell presented the club’s letter of permission, dated eleven years earlier. He read it with the care usually reserved for parking tickets.

“This gives you Tuesday evenings in Room Four.”

“Precisely.”

“This is Room Four.”

Behind him, a woman lay on a cylinder and made an expression Ahmed recognized.

The only vacant space was the assembly hall, but Vale wouldn’t unlock it. A retirement party was booked there at noon tomorrow. The floor had been polished. Forty chairs stood in straight rows.

“We would require eight chairs,” said Mrs. Bell. “Our movements are largely theoretical.”

Vale looked at the chess bags, then at Derek’s takeaway coffee.

Derek held it behind his back, where it immediately leaked onto his trousers.

“No drinks,” Vale said.

“Agreed,” said Derek, with feeling.

The bargaining improved once Ahmed asked what had to be ready for the party. Vale produced a diagram. Six tables, forty chairs, a clear aisle to the fire exit. He was alone tonight; his assistant’s bus had broken down.

“We can set it up afterward,” Ahmed said.

Mrs. Bell examined the diagram. “That aisle won’t work. The gift table blocks the door when it opens.”

Vale examined it too. He turned the paper sideways, then back. “You’re right.”

Nobody celebrated. This was the first useful silence of the evening.

They agreed on ninety minutes, eight chairs, felt pads under every table leg, and the retirement arrangement completed before departure. Vale wrote the conditions on the back of an old raffle flyer. Mrs. Bell signed. Derek signed as witness, though nobody had requested one.

It was seven when Vale unlocked the hall. They tipped the tables to fit the pads, then set out the eight chairs.

At eight, Ahmed lost his queen while calculating the width of the aisle. At eight thirty, everybody helped. Derek carried chairs with his wet trouser leg turned discreetly toward the wall.

Vale tested the exit and walked between the tables. Then he opened his booking ledger.

“Next Tuesday, same conditions. Temporary.”

Mrs. Bell put the raffle flyer into her chess case beside the eleven-year-old letter.

“Temporary,” she repeated. “An excellent opening.”

The greenhouse had been made from six discarded windows and the clear roof of a bus shelter. Ruth called it the conservatory. Nobody else did, but nobody corrected her.

In October they agreed to run the heater from ten until six. Ruth grew salad for herself and her husband; Dev was raising tomato plants to sell in spring; Marion kept cuttings from the garden she had left when she moved into the flats. Each paid ten pounds a month. The cable passed through Marion's kitchen window because hers was nearest.

In January she brought the bill downstairs in its envelope.

Dev cleared a dry patch on the potting bench. He had a calculator on his telephone. Ruth took off her gardening gloves finger by finger.

Marion's tariff charged more at night. She had chosen it because she was usually out in the daytime and it had looked cheaper overall. The extra electricity came to forty-seven pounds, after their contributions.

"You should have said," Ruth told her.

"I thought ten pounds was ten pounds."

Dev looked at the heater's label. "I should have checked this."

He offered to pay the difference, then explained that he could not do it until the plants sold. Ruth said she could manage another five. Her husband had begun leaving the television off during breakfast, which she mentioned as though it were merely a change in habit.

Marion folded the bill along its existing crease. She had already taken the forty-seven from the money for visiting her daughter.

They discussed extending a cable from Dev's flat. It would cross the common path. They discussed turning the heater off, and stood looking at the trays while the heater clicked on beside their ankles.

"Twelve degrees," Dev said eventually. "Instead of sixteen. I can bring the tomatoes indoors."

His living room was small; Marion had seen it when she went to feed his cat. She knew where the trays would have to go.

They lowered the thermostat. Ruth paid her five immediately. Dev wrote the balance, due when the plants sold in spring, on the back of the seed catalogue and gave Marion the page.

"An hour with it off, an hour with it on," Dev said. "Read the meter before and after each. Leave your other appliances the same. We can use your night rate and the hours it runs to work out next month's shares."

Marion agreed to the estimate, but wanted the shares weekly in advance. Nobody suggested she should finance the difference again.

That evening Marion unplugged the heater while Ruth held the torch. They put its cable through a cheap timer Marion had bought that afternoon, so it could not run past six.

The timer was another six pounds. Marion kept its receipt in the envelope.
